title: Claude Code vs Codex (2026): pricing, free tier and which to pick
description: Claude Code vs OpenAI Codex compared: plan prices and free access as of Oct 2026, best use cases, strengths, drawbacks and FAQs.
answer: Claude Code and OpenAI Codex are both coding agents that come bundled with their maker's chat subscription, so the real choice is usually which ecosystem you already pay for. As of Oct 2026, Codex has a $0 entry point through ChatGPT Free (one model, in the desktop app, subject to rollout), while Claude Code is not part of Claude's Free plan and starts with Claude Pro. At the $20/month level the two cost the same if you pay monthly, and both offer higher tiers from $100/month for heavy use. In our view, try each on a real task from your own codebase before committing, because usage limits on both depend on the model and task size rather than a fixed message count.

rows.price: Not on the Free plan. Claude Pro $17/month with annual billing ($200 up front) or $20 billed monthly; Max from $100/month.
rows.bestFor: In our view: developers who already use Claude and want one subscription for chat and coding.
rows.strength: Included in every paid Claude plan; coding and chat share one usage pool, and heavy users can switch to pay-as-you-go API credits.
rows.drawback: No free access. Usage resets in five-hour windows, with weekly limits on paid plans.

rows.price: ChatGPT Free $0 and Go $8/month (one model, desktop app, subject to rollout); Plus $20/month; Pro from $100/month ($100, $200 or $500 options). API-key use billed at API rates.
rows.bestFor: In our view: ChatGPT subscribers, and teams that want to script an agent in CI with an API key.
rows.strength: A $0 way to try it; on Plus it runs on the web, in the CLI, in an IDE extension and on iOS, and an API-key mode suits automation.
rows.drawback: Free and Go get a single model in the desktop app only; API-key use has no cloud features such as GitHub code review or Slack.

pick: Pick Claude Code if you already pay for Claude Pro or Max, or plan to, and want your coding work to draw from the same plan as your chats.
Pick Codex if you want to start for $0, already pay for ChatGPT Plus or Pro, or need an API-key setup for CI pipelines.
In our view, if neither ecosystem matters to you, run both on the same small feature for a week before choosing.

faqs.q: Is Claude Code free?
faqs.a: No. As of Oct 2026, Claude's pricing page lists Claude Code as not included on the Free plan. It is included with Pro ($17/month billed annually or $20 monthly) and Max (from $100/month). Check the vendor's site for current pricing.

faqs.q: Is OpenAI Codex free?
faqs.a: There is a limited free option. As of Oct 2026, ChatGPT Free ($0) includes one model in the Codex desktop app, subject to rollout. Plus ($20/month) adds the web, CLI, IDE extension and iOS. Check the vendor's site for current pricing.

faqs.q: Can I use either one with an API key instead of a subscription?
faqs.a: Codex's pricing page describes an API-key mode billed at API rates, without the cloud features. Claude's pricing FAQ says heavy coding users can switch to pay-as-you-go API credits through a Console account.

faqs.q: Which is cheaper for daily use?
faqs.a: At list prices both are $20/month when billed monthly (Claude Pro, ChatGPT Plus), and both have tiers from $100/month. In our view the cheaper option is whichever one's usage limits fit your workload, which you can only learn by trying it.

title: Cursor vs Claude Code vs Codex (2026): pricing and which to pick
h1: Cursor vs Claude Code vs Codex
description: Cursor, Claude Code and OpenAI Codex compared side by side: plan prices and free access as of Oct 2026, best for, strengths, drawbacks and FAQs.
answer: Cursor is an AI-first code editor with a built-in agent, while Claude Code and OpenAI Codex are agents tied to the Claude and ChatGPT subscriptions. As of Oct 2026, Cursor and Codex both have a $0 plan with limited usage, and Claude Code starts with Claude Pro. Cursor's paid plans start at $8/month (Grok models only) and its Premium plan is $30/month, with third-party models billed separately at API list price. In our view, choose Cursor if you want the agent built into your editor, and Claude Code or Codex if you prefer a model maker's own agent bundled with chat. In our view, using an editor and a separate agent together is also a reasonable setup.

rows.price: Free $0 (limited agent and chat requests); Plus $8/month (Grok models only); Premium $30/month; Super $100/month; Ultra $200/month; Teams from $30/user/month. Third-party models billed separately at API list price.
rows.bestFor: In our view: developers who want the agent inside an editor rather than in a separate tool.
rows.strength: The agent is on every plan, including Free; Premium and up add cloud agents and automations, code hosting and AI code reviews.
rows.drawback: Plan prices cover Grok models; other providers' models cost extra at API list price, so totals can be harder to predict.

rows.price: Not on the Free plan. Claude Pro $17/month with annual billing or $20 monthly; Max from $100/month.
rows.bestFor: In our view: Claude users who want one subscription for chat and coding.
rows.strength: Included in all paid Claude plans and shares a usage pool with Claude chat; pay-as-you-go API credits are an option for heavy use.
rows.drawback: No free access; usage resets in five-hour windows, with weekly limits on paid plans.

rows.price: ChatGPT Free $0 and Go $8/month (one model, desktop app, subject to rollout); Plus $20/month; Pro from $100/month. API-key use billed at API rates.
rows.bestFor: In our view: ChatGPT subscribers and teams automating coding tasks in CI.
rows.strength: Runs on the web, CLI, IDE extension and iOS on Plus, plus an API-key mode for scripts and CI.
rows.drawback: Free and Go are limited to one model in the desktop app; API-key use has no cloud features.

pick: Pick Cursor if you want an editor-first workflow and like having cloud agents and code reviews in the same product.
Pick Claude Code if you already pay for Claude, or want coding and chat on one Anthropic plan.
Pick Codex if you want a $0 starting point inside ChatGPT, or need API-key automation in CI.
In our view, an editor plus one agent is a common and reasonable setup, so this doesn't have to be an either-or decision.

faqs.q: Which of the three has a free plan?
faqs.a: As of Oct 2026, Cursor has a Free plan with limited agent and chat requests, and Codex is available on ChatGPT Free with one model in the desktop app. Claude's Free plan does not include Claude Code. Check the vendor's site for current pricing.

faqs.q: What is the cheapest paid option?
faqs.a: At list prices as of Oct 2026: Cursor Plus and ChatGPT Go are both $8/month, but Cursor Plus is limited to Grok models and Go is limited to one model in the Codex desktop app. Claude Pro is $17/month billed annually.

faqs.q: Can I use Claude or OpenAI models inside Cursor?
faqs.a: Cursor's pricing page says third-party models are available on Premium and above at API list price, billed separately by usage. The Plus plan includes Grok models only.

faqs.q: Do I need an editor if I use Claude Code or Codex?
faqs.a: Not necessarily, but in our view most people still review and edit code in an editor. Codex lists an IDE extension on its Plus plan.

title: n8n vs Make vs Zapier (2026): pricing, free plans and which to pick
description: n8n, Make and Zapier compared: free plans, starting prices and billing units as of Oct 2026, plus best for, strengths, drawbacks and FAQs.
answer: All three build automated workflows between apps, but they bill differently. n8n charges per full workflow run (an execution) no matter how many steps it has, and offers a free self-hosted Community Edition. Make bills in credits, with most actions using one credit and 1,000 free credits a month. Zapier bills in tasks, with each successful step using a task, and its Free plan gives 100 tasks a month for two-step Zaps. In our view, n8n suits technical users who want self-hosting or long multi-step workflows, Make suits people who like a visual canvas and a usable free plan, and Zapier suits those who want the widest choice of ready-made app connections with the least setup.

rows.price: Free self-hosted Community Edition. Cloud: Starter €20/month and Pro €50/month (billed annually); Business €667/month billed annually (self-hosted). Cloud free trial includes 1,000 executions, no card needed.
rows.bestFor: In our view: developers and technical teams who want to self-host or run complex AI and agent workflows.
rows.strength: Priced per complete workflow run regardless of step count; all plans include unlimited users, workflows and integrations.
rows.drawback: No free hosted plan beyond the trial. In our view the learning curve is steeper for non-technical users.

rows.price: Free plan with 1,000 credits/month; paid Core, Pro, Teams and Enterprise plans priced by credit volume, cheaper when paid annually. We couldn't verify paid plan prices on the pricing page today.
rows.bestFor: In our view: visual thinkers building multi-step scenarios on a budget.
rows.strength: A free plan with monthly credits, a visual scenario builder, and integrations with more than 1,000 apps.
rows.drawback: Each module action uses credits, so one complex run can use many; scenarios pause when credits run out.

rows.price: Free $0 (100 tasks/month, two-step Zaps); Professional from $19.99/month billed annually ($29.99 monthly) for 750 tasks; Team from $69/month billed annually for 2,000 tasks; Enterprise custom.
rows.bestFor: In our view: non-technical teams that need to connect many popular apps quickly.
rows.strength: Connects 9,000+ apps; a 14-day Professional trial needs no card; triggers and built-in tools like Filter and Formatter don't use tasks.
rows.drawback: The Free plan is limited to two-step Zaps, and costs rise with task volume since each successful action step counts.

pick: Pick n8n if you are comfortable with a technical tool and want self-hosting, or your workflows have many steps and you'd rather pay per run.
Pick Make if you want a visual builder and a free plan with enough monthly credits to run real scenarios.
Pick Zapier if you need a specific app integration that the others lack, or want the simplest setup for a non-technical team.
In our view, estimate how many steps and runs your main workflow needs per month, then price it on each vendor's pricing page before deciding.

faqs.q: Is n8n free?
faqs.a: The self-hosted Community Edition is available on GitHub at no cost. As of Oct 2026, n8n's cloud plans start at €20/month billed annually, with a free trial. Check the vendor's site for current pricing.

faqs.q: Which has the best free plan?
faqs.a: It depends on your workflow. As of Oct 2026, Make's Free plan includes 1,000 credits a month, and Zapier's Free plan includes 100 tasks a month for two-step Zaps. n8n's free option is self-hosting. In our view Make's free plan is the most generous for multi-step workflows.

faqs.q: How do executions, credits and tasks differ?
faqs.a: n8n counts one execution per full workflow run. Make counts credits per module action, with most actions using one credit. Zapier counts a task for each successful action step, while triggers and its built-in tools don't count.

faqs.q: Can I self-host Make or Zapier?
faqs.a: Neither pricing page describes a self-hosted option. n8n offers self-hosting through its Community Edition and its Business plan.

title: Lovable vs Base44 vs Replit (2026): free plans, pricing and which to pick
description: Lovable, Base44 and Replit compared as AI app builders: free plans and prices as of Oct 2026, best for, strengths, drawbacks and FAQs.
answer: Lovable, Base44 and Replit all turn a chat prompt into a working web app, and all three have a free plan as of Oct 2026. Lovable gives 5 build credits a day on its free plan and prices paid plans by credits rather than seats. Base44 includes a backend, database and user auth on every plan, with paid plans from $16/month billed annually. Replit runs a full browser-based development environment with hosting, with Core at $20/month ($18 billed annually). In our view, Lovable and Base44 suit people who want to stay in chat and avoid code, while Replit suits people who expect to look at and edit the code themselves.

rows.price: Free: 5 build credits/day (up to 30/month) plus 20 Cloud credits/month. Paid Pro and Business plans are priced by credits; we couldn't verify their prices on the pricing page today.
rows.bestFor: In our view: non-developers and small teams building websites and web apps by chat.
rows.strength: No per-seat pricing: unlimited workspace members share one credit pool, and you own the code you build.
rows.drawback: Credit cost per message varies with task complexity, so spend can be hard to predict; unused credits expire.

rows.price: Free: 25 message credits/month, up to 5 apps. Paid plans from Starter $16/month billed annually (100 message credits) up to Elite $160/month billed annually; yearly billing saves 20%.
rows.bestFor: In our view: founders and teams building internal tools or customer portals that need login and data.
rows.strength: Backend, database, authentication and analytics are included on every plan, including Free.
rows.drawback: The free plan is small (25 message credits a month), and GitHub integration starts above the Starter plan.

rows.price: Free Starter plan (daily Agent credits up to a monthly cap); Core $20/month ($18 billed annually); Pro $100/month ($90 billed annually); Enterprise via sales.
rows.bestFor: In our view: builders who want an agent plus a full coding environment they can take over.
rows.strength: Building, databases and publishing live in one browser workspace; Pro supports up to 15 collaborators.
rows.drawback: The free plan only offers Lite build and one published app that goes offline after 30 days; third-party connectors need Core.

pick: Pick Lovable if you want to build websites and web apps purely by chat, especially as a team sharing one credit balance.
Pick Base44 if your app needs sign-in, a database and integrations from day one and you'd rather not set them up yourself.
Pick Replit if you want to see and edit the code, or plan to grow the project into a fuller software build.
In our view, build the same small app on each free plan first; the free tiers are enough to see which workflow you prefer.

faqs.q: Which has the most generous free plan?
faqs.a: They measure usage differently. As of Oct 2026, Lovable's free plan gives 5 build credits a day (up to 30 a month), Base44's gives 25 message credits a month for up to 5 apps, and Replit's Starter plan gives daily Agent credits up to a monthly cap plus one published app. Check the vendor's site for current pricing.

faqs.q: Do I own the code?
faqs.a: Lovable and Base44 both state on their pricing pages that you own what you build, and Base44 describes two-way GitHub sync for exporting source code. Replit projects are code you can open and edit in the workspace.

faqs.q: Which is best for apps with user accounts and a database?
faqs.a: In our view Base44 makes this easiest, since its pricing page lists authentication and database features on every plan. Replit includes production databases among its cloud credits, and Lovable apps run on its Cloud with an included monthly grant.

faqs.q: Do any of them charge per seat?
faqs.a: Lovable says it doesn't charge per seat; workspaces have unlimited members sharing credits. Base44 and Replit price by plan; Replit's Pro plan supports up to 15 collaborators.

title: Best vector database for RAG (2026): Pinecone vs Qdrant vs Weaviate vs Chroma
description: Pinecone, Qdrant, Weaviate and Chroma compared for RAG: free tiers, starting prices and limits as of Oct 2026, plus which to pick and FAQs.
answer: There is no single best vector database for retrieval-augmented generation (RAG); the right one depends on whether you want to run servers, how much data you have and how much you want to spend. All four here have a free option as of Oct 2026. Pinecone is fully managed with a free Starter plan and paid plans from $20/month. Qdrant and Weaviate are open source with managed clouds that each have a free tier. Chroma is open source and its cloud bills purely by usage after a $0 Starter plan. In our view, Chroma is the quickest way to prototype, Pinecone is the simplest if you never want to manage infrastructure, and Qdrant or Weaviate are strong picks if you want the option to self-host later.

rows.price: Starter free (up to 2 GB storage, 2M write units and 1M read units a month); Builder $20/month flat; Standard $50/month minimum usage, with a 3-week trial including $300 credits; Enterprise $500/month minimum.
rows.bestFor: In our view: teams that want a managed service with no servers to run.
rows.strength: Fully managed, with dense, sparse and full-text indexes plus hosted embedding and reranking models on every plan.
rows.drawback: The free Starter plan runs only on AWS us-east-1 with up to 5 indexes; production costs on Standard are usage-based.

rows.price: Open-source version available. Cloud Free tier 'free forever' (single node, 0.5 vCPU, 1 GB RAM, 4 GB disk); Standard tier usage-based, billed hourly; Premium tier has a minimum spend.
rows.bestFor: In our view: developers who want open source today with a managed or hybrid cloud path later.
rows.strength: Run it yourself, in Qdrant's cloud, or as managed clusters in your own infrastructure (Hybrid Cloud).
rows.drawback: The free tier is a single node without high availability, and resource-based cloud pricing takes some estimating.

rows.price: Free $0/month (1 cluster per user, 100,000 objects, 1 GB memory, 10 GB disk, 1 collection); Flex from $45/month pay-as-you-go; Premium prepaid, from $400/month.
rows.bestFor: In our view: RAG apps that need hybrid search and multi-tenancy.
rows.strength: Hybrid search and multi-tenancy on every plan, including Free, plus a built-in embeddings service.
rows.drawback: The free tier allows one collection and 100,000 objects; pricing by vector dimensions takes some math to estimate.

rows.price: Open source. Cloud Starter $0/month plus usage, with $5 free credits; Team $250/month plus usage ($100 credits). Usage: $2.50/GiB written, $0.33/GiB-month stored, $0.0075/TiB queried.
rows.bestFor: In our view: prototypes and small projects, especially running locally.
rows.strength: Open source, and in our view easy to start with; the cloud has no fixed fee on Starter, just usage.
rows.drawback: In our view, scaling a self-hosted setup takes work, and the jump from Starter to Team ($250/month) is steep for small teams.

pick: Pick Chroma if you're prototyping a RAG app and want something you can run locally in minutes.
Pick Pinecone if you want a hosted service and don't want to think about servers, clusters or scaling.
Pick Qdrant if you want open source with a clear path to managed, hybrid or private cloud deployments.
Pick Weaviate if hybrid search, multi-tenancy or built-in embeddings matter for your app.
In our view, all four handle typical RAG workloads, so try your own data on two free tiers before you commit.

faqs.q: Which vector database is free?
faqs.a: All four have a free option as of Oct 2026: Pinecone's Starter plan, Qdrant's Free tier, Weaviate's Free plan and Chroma's $0 Starter plan (plus usage, with free credits). Qdrant, Weaviate and Chroma can also be self-hosted. Check the vendor's site for current pricing.

faqs.q: Which is best for RAG in production?
faqs.a: In our view, any of the four can serve production RAG. Pinecone, Qdrant, Weaviate and Chroma each list uptime or support SLAs on at least some paid tiers. Choose based on whether you want fully managed or self-hostable, and on your data size.

faqs.q: Can I self-host?
faqs.a: Qdrant, Weaviate and Chroma are open source and can be self-hosted. Pinecone offers a Bring Your Own Cloud option that runs Pinecone in your cloud account, which is a managed service rather than self-hosting.

faqs.q: What's the cheapest way to start?
faqs.a: Use a free tier. As of Oct 2026, Pinecone's Starter includes up to 2 GB storage, Qdrant's Free tier includes 4 GB disk, Weaviate's Free plan allows 100,000 objects, and Chroma's Starter plan includes $5 in free credits.

title: Railway vs Vercel vs Render (2026): pricing, free plans and which to pick
description: Railway, Vercel and Render compared for hosting apps and databases: free plans, plan fees and usage billing as of Nov 2026, plus best for, strengths, drawbacks and FAQs.
answer: All three deploy your code from Git, but they are built around different workloads. Vercel centers on frontends and serverless functions with a global CDN, Railway runs long-lived services and databases billed per second for the resources they use, and Render offers web services, workers, cron jobs and managed Postgres on fixed-size instances. As of Nov 2026, each has a $0 entry point: Vercel Hobby (personal, non-commercial use only), Railway's Free plan with $1 of monthly usage, and Render's Hobby workspace with free compute instances. Paid plans start at $5/month on Railway (Hobby), $20/month on Vercel Pro and $25/month on Render Pro, before usage or compute. In our view, Vercel fits frontend-heavy web apps, Railway fits small backends and side projects that need a database next to the app, and Render fits teams that want predictable per-instance prices.

rows.price: Free Trial: $5 one-time credit for 30 days, no card. Free $0/month with $1 of monthly usage. Hobby $5/month including $5 of usage. Pro $20/month per workspace including $20 of usage. Usage above the included amount is billed per second.
rows.bestFor: In our view: solo developers and small teams running APIs, workers and databases side by side.
rows.strength: Per-second billing for CPU, memory and disk, so stopped services cost nothing; Pro seats are included in the workspace fee.
rows.drawback: Costs move with usage, so bills are less predictable than a fixed instance price; the Free plan allows one project and no custom domains.

rows.price: Hobby $0/month (personal, non-commercial use). Pro $20/month with a $20 monthly usage credit; developer seats are listed at $20/month each. Enterprise custom.
rows.bestFor: In our view: frontend and full-stack web apps (for example Next.js) that benefit from a global CDN and preview deployments.
rows.strength: Git-based deploys with preview URLs, a built-in CDN and serverless functions, with included Hobby quotas such as 100 GB/month of data transfer.
rows.drawback: Hobby is limited to personal, non-commercial use, and it doesn't host a database itself; databases come from Marketplace integrations.

rows.price: Hobby workspace $0/month plus compute, with free web service, Postgres and Key Value instances (usage limits apply). Pro $25/month plus compute; Scale $499/month plus compute. Paid web services from $7/month; paid Postgres from $6/month.
rows.bestFor: In our view: teams that want web services, workers, cron jobs and Postgres on one platform with fixed instance prices.
rows.strength: Clear per-instance prices for services, Postgres and Key Value, plus cron jobs, background workers and infrastructure-as-code blueprints on every plan.
rows.drawback: You pay a workspace fee and compute separately; horizontal autoscaling and full-stack previews require Pro or above.

pick: Pick Vercel if your app is mostly frontend plus serverless functions and you want preview deployments on every push.
Pick Railway if you want an app server and its database in one project and prefer paying only for the resources you actually use.
Pick Render if you want fixed monthly prices per service and a managed Postgres without usage-based surprises.
In our view, combining them is common: for example a Vercel frontend talking to an API and database hosted on Railway or Render.

faqs.q: Which of the three is free?
faqs.a: As of Nov 2026, all three have a $0 option. Vercel Hobby is free for personal, non-commercial projects. Railway's Free plan includes $1 of usage a month, and new users get a one-time $5 trial credit. Render's Hobby workspace is $0 and offers free web service, Postgres and Key Value instances with usage limits. Check each vendor's site for current pricing.

faqs.q: Can I host a database on each of them?
faqs.a: Render offers managed Postgres and Redis-compatible Key Value. Railway runs databases as services billed by the same CPU, memory and volume rates as your app. Vercel doesn't host a database itself; its pricing page lists storage such as Blob, and databases are added through Marketplace integrations.

faqs.q: Can I use Vercel Hobby for a commercial site?
faqs.a: No. Vercel's pricing FAQ says Hobby is for personal, non-commercial use, and Pro is meant for professional and business use.

faqs.q: How does Railway billing differ from Render?
faqs.a: Railway meters CPU, memory and disk per second and subtracts your plan's included usage. Render charges a fixed monthly price per instance size, prorated by the second, on top of the workspace plan fee.

title: Best Cursor alternatives (Nov 2026): after the X Subscription pricing change
description: Cursor alternatives compared after Cursor's October 2026 move to The X Subscription: Windsurf, Claude Code, Codex, GitHub Copilot and Cline, with prices as of Nov 2026.
answer: In October 2026, Cursor became part of The X Subscription, a combined plan for Grok, Cursor and X. On the new plans, third-party models such as Claude, GPT and Gemini are no longer part of the included usage: Plus ($8/month) is limited to Cursor's own Grok and Composer models, and Premium ($30/month) and above can use third-party models only at API list price from prepaid credit. Existing subscribers can keep their legacy Cursor plans for now. If you want a bundled allowance for other vendors' models, the main alternatives as of Nov 2026 are Windsurf (Pro $20/month, includes frontier models from several providers), Claude Code (with Claude Pro, $20/month or $17/month billed annually), OpenAI Codex (included in ChatGPT, including Free and Go), GitHub Copilot (Pro $10/month) and Cline (free, open-source, you pay your model provider). In our view, the right choice depends on whether you want an editor like Cursor or a separate agent, and which model vendor you prefer.

rows.price: Free $0/month (light quota); Pro $20/month; Max $200/month; Teams $80/month plus $40/month per full developer seat.
rows.bestFor: In our view: people who want the closest thing to Cursor, an AI editor with tab completions, but with other vendors' models in the plan.
rows.strength: Pro includes access to frontier models from OpenAI, Anthropic, Google and SpaceXAI, plus unlimited Tab completions on every plan.
rows.drawback: Usage beyond the plan's daily and weekly allowance is bought at API pricing, and the Free plan has limited model availability.

rows.price: Not on the Free plan. Claude Pro $17/month billed annually ($200 up front) or $20 monthly; Max $100/month; Ultra $200/month.
rows.bestFor: In our view: developers who mainly want Claude models and are comfortable with a terminal-first agent.
rows.strength: Included in every paid Claude plan, sharing one usage pool with Claude chat; Max and Ultra add monthly API credits.
rows.drawback: No free access, and usage limits reset on five-hour and weekly windows rather than a fixed message count.

rows.price: ChatGPT Free $0 and Go $8/month (one model in the desktop app, subject to rollout); Plus $20/month; Pro from $100/month ($100, $200 or $500). API-key use billed at API rates.
rows.bestFor: In our view: ChatGPT subscribers and anyone who wants a $0 or $8 way to try a coding agent.
rows.strength: Runs on the web, in the CLI, in an IDE extension and on iOS on Plus, plus an API-key mode for CI and scripts.
rows.drawback: Free and Go are limited to one model in the desktop app; API-key mode has no cloud features such as GitHub code review.

rows.price: Free $0 (limited chat and agent usage); Pro $10/month; Pro+ $39/month; Max $100/month. Chat and agents use monthly GitHub AI Credits.
rows.bestFor: In our view: developers who want to stay in their existing editor and work closely with GitHub.
rows.strength: Code completions and next-edit suggestions don't use credits, and the Free plan supports the CLI and agent mode.
rows.drawback: Chat and agent work draws down AI Credits at $0.01 each, so heavy agent use can need a paid budget on top of the plan.

rows.price: Free open-source extension for individual developers; you pay only for AI inference, with your own API keys or the Cline provider. Enterprise is via sales.
rows.bestFor: In our view: developers who want full control over which model they use and what they pay for it.
rows.strength: No subscription or seat fee for individuals, and it works with many providers including Anthropic, OpenAI, Google and OpenRouter.
rows.drawback: Costs depend entirely on your model usage, which can be hard to predict on long agent runs.

pick: Stay on Cursor if you're happy with Cursor's own Grok and Composer models, or you're on a legacy plan that still includes third-party usage.
Pick Windsurf if you want another AI editor with other vendors' models included in a $20/month plan.
Pick Claude Code or Codex if you already pay for Claude or ChatGPT and want the model maker's own agent.
Pick GitHub Copilot if you want to keep your current editor, or Cline if you'd rather bring your own API keys and pay only for usage.

User reports (not verified by us): in recent Reddit and Hacker News threads collected by last30days.ai, some long-time Cursor users say they cancelled over the plan and model changes, while others say the cheaper plans still cover their daily use. In our view, try an alternative on a real task before switching.

faqs.q: What changed in Cursor's plans in October 2026?
faqs.a: Cursor's forum announcement (posted October 12, 2026, UTC) introduced The X Subscription, which bundles Grok, Cursor and X. On these plans, included usage covers Cursor's own models; third-party models are not included and are available on Premium ($30/month) and above at API list price from prepaid credit. Existing Cursor subscribers can keep their current plans.

faqs.q: Is there a Cursor Plus plan, and what does it include?
faqs.a: Yes. As of Nov 2026, Cursor's pricing page lists Plus at $8/month. It includes Cursor's agent with Grok and Composer models only, at fixed settings, plus Grok and X features. Cloud agents, Bugbot code reviews and third-party models need Premium or above.

faqs.q: Which Cursor alternative is cheapest?
faqs.a: At list prices as of Nov 2026: Cline is free (you pay your model provider), Codex is included in ChatGPT Free and Go ($8/month) with one model in the desktop app, and GitHub Copilot has a Free plan and Pro at $10/month. Check each vendor's site for current pricing.

faqs.q: Are people really leaving Cursor?

title: Best vibe coding tools (Nov 2026): prompt-to-app builders compared
description: The best vibe coding tools for building apps from a prompt: Lovable, Bolt, v0, Replit and Emergent compared, with free plans and prices as of Nov 2026.
answer: Vibe coding means describing an app in plain language and letting an AI agent write, run and deploy the code while you steer by chat. Lovable, Bolt, v0, Replit and Emergent all work this way in the browser. As of Nov 2026, Lovable, Bolt, v0 and Emergent have $0 plans; Bolt Pro is $25/month, Emergent Standard is $20/month ($17 billed annually), Replit Core is $20/month ($18 billed annually), and v0 Business is $100/user/month. Most of them meter usage in credits or tokens, so the real cost depends on how much you build. In our view, Lovable and Bolt are the easiest starting points for non-developers, v0 suits React and Next.js projects headed for Vercel, Replit suits people who want a full coding workspace, and Emergent suits builders who want web and mobile apps from one tool.

rows.bestFor: In our view: non-developers building websites and web apps by chat.
rows.strength: No per-seat pricing: everyone in a workspace shares one credit pool, and you own the code you build.
rows.drawback: Credit cost per message varies with task complexity, and unused monthly credits expire.

rows.price: Free: 1M tokens/month with a 300K daily limit. Pro $25/month billed monthly (10M tokens/month, rollover). Teams $30/month per member. Enterprise custom.
rows.bestFor: In our view: quick prototypes and small web apps with hosting included.
rows.strength: Free plan includes hosting and unlimited databases; Pro adds custom domains and rolls unused tokens over.
rows.drawback: Free sites carry Bolt branding, and the free daily token limit can cut long sessions short.

rows.price: Free $0/month with a 7 message/day limit; paid Plus plan; Business $100/user/month. Model usage billed per token from included credits.
rows.bestFor: In our view: React and Next.js UIs and apps that will be deployed on Vercel.
rows.strength: Free plan includes deploying to Vercel, GitHub sync and visual editing with Design Mode.
rows.drawback: The Free plan's 7 messages a day is tight for real projects, and paid usage is token-based.

rows.price: Core $20/month ($18 billed annually); Pro $100/month ($90 billed annually); Enterprise via sales.
rows.bestFor: In our view: builders who want an agent plus a full coding environment they can take over.
rows.strength: Building, databases and publishing live in one browser workspace, and you can edit the code directly.
rows.drawback: We couldn't confirm a $0 plan on the pricing page today; Core includes $20 and Pro $100 toward more powerful models, so heavy use can cost more.

rows.price: Free $0/month with 10 credits/month; Standard $20/month ($17/month billed annually, 100 credits/month); Pro $200/month ($167/month billed annually, 750 credits/month); Enterprise custom.

pick: Pick Lovable if you've never coded and want the simplest chat-to-website path.
Pick Bolt if you want a generous free token allowance and hosting for quick prototypes.
Pick v0 if you're building React or Next.js and plan to deploy on Vercel.
Pick Replit if you expect to open the code and keep developing it yourself, or Emergent if you need a mobile app too.
In our view, vibe-coded apps still need a human review of security, data handling and costs before real users touch them.

faqs.q: What is vibe coding?
faqs.a: It's building software by describing what you want in plain language and letting an AI agent write and change the code, while you test the result and give feedback by chat rather than editing code line by line.

faqs.q: Which vibe coding tools are free?
faqs.a: As of Nov 2026, Lovable (5 build credits a day), Bolt (1M tokens a month), v0 (7 messages a day) and Emergent (10 credits a month) all list a $0 plan. Check each vendor's site for current pricing.

faqs.q: Can I export the code?
faqs.a: Lovable's pricing FAQ says you own the code you build, v0 lists GitHub sync on its Free plan, Replit gives you the full project in its workspace, and Emergent lists GitHub integration on Standard and above. Bolt's pricing page doesn't cover code export, so check its docs.

title: Lovable vs Bolt (2026): free plans, pricing and which to pick
description: Lovable vs Bolt compared as AI app builders: free plans, paid plans and how usage is metered as of Nov 2026, plus best for, strengths, drawbacks and FAQs.
answer: Lovable and Bolt both build web apps from a chat prompt in the browser and both have free plans, but they meter usage differently. As of Nov 2026, Lovable's free plan gives 5 build credits a day (up to 30 a month) plus 20 Cloud credits a month, and its paid plans are priced by shared workspace credits rather than seats. Bolt's free plan gives 1M tokens a month with a 300K daily limit, Pro is $25/month with 10M tokens and rollover, and Teams is $30/month per member. In our view, Lovable suits non-technical builders and teams who want one shared credit pool, while Bolt suits people who like a token allowance they can see and carry over, and who may want to pick their own database provider.

rows.price: Free: 5 build credits/day (up to 30/month) plus 20 Cloud credits/month. Paid plans are priced by credits; we couldn't verify their prices on the pricing page today.
rows.bestFor: In our view: non-developers and teams building websites and web apps by chat.
rows.strength: Unlimited workspace members share one credit pool, so adding people doesn't add seat fees; Plan Mode costs 1 credit per message.
rows.drawback: Default-mode credit cost varies with task complexity; monthly plan credits expire two months after issue.

rows.price: Free: 1M tokens/month with a 300K daily limit. Pro $25/month billed monthly (10M tokens/month, rollover). Teams $30/month per member. Enterprise custom.

title: Supabase vs Firebase vs Convex (2026): free tiers, pricing and which to pick
description: Supabase, Firebase and Convex compared as app backends: free tiers, paid plans and data models as of Nov 2026, plus best for, strengths, drawbacks and FAQs.
answer: Supabase, Firebase and Convex are all backend platforms that give an app a database, auth, file storage and server functions, but their data models differ. Supabase is built on Postgres (SQL), Firebase centers on the NoSQL Firestore and Realtime Database from Google, and Convex is a reactive database where queries and server functions are written in TypeScript. As of Nov 2026, all three have a free tier: Supabase Free ($0, 500 MB database, paused after a week of inactivity), Firebase's no-cost Spark plan, and Convex Free & Starter. Paid entry points are Supabase Pro from $25/month, Firebase's pay-as-you-go Blaze plan, and Convex Professional at $25 per developer/month. In our view, Supabase fits teams that want SQL and Postgres tools, Firebase fits mobile apps already using Google services, and Convex fits TypeScript apps that need live-updating data.

rows.price: Free $0/month (500 MB database, 50,000 MAUs; projects paused after 1 week of inactivity; 2 active projects). Pro from $25/month including $10 of compute credits. Team from $599/month. Enterprise custom.
rows.bestFor: In our view: apps that want a real Postgres database with SQL, plus auth and storage in one place.
rows.strength: A standard Postgres database you can connect to with any Postgres client or ORM; unlimited API requests on every plan; can be self-hosted.
rows.drawback: Free projects pause after a week of inactivity, and each extra project on a paid plan adds its own compute cost.

rows.price: Spark plan: no cost, no payment method needed, with quotas (for example Firestore 1 GiB stored, 50K reads/day, 20K writes/day). Blaze plan: pay as you go above the no-cost usage; eligible new users can get $300 in Google Cloud credit.
rows.bestFor: In our view: mobile and web apps that want Google's SDKs, push messaging, analytics and crash reporting alongside the database.
rows.strength: Many products are no-cost on both plans, including Analytics, Crashlytics and Cloud Messaging, and Blaze keeps the Spark no-cost usage.
rows.drawback: Usage is billed per read, write and GB, so costs need monitoring; Cloud Functions and some other products need the Blaze plan.

rows.price: Free & Starter $0/month (Starter is pay-as-you-go beyond the free limits, e.g. 1M function calls and 0.5 GB database storage included). Professional $25 per developer/month. Business & Enterprise from a $2,500 monthly minimum.
rows.bestFor: In our view: TypeScript and React apps that need data to update live on screen without extra plumbing.
rows.strength: Reactive queries, file storage, text and vector search, crons and auth are included on every plan, with no charge for query and mutation compute.
rows.drawback: Priced per developer on Professional, and it uses its own database model rather than SQL, so moving away takes more work.

pick: Pick Supabase if you want Postgres and SQL, or the option to self-host later.
Pick Firebase if you're building a mobile app and want Google's analytics, messaging and crash reporting in the same console.
Pick Convex if you write TypeScript and want real-time, reactive data with backend logic in the same codebase.
In our view, the data model matters more than the free tier: relational data leans Supabase, document data leans Firebase, and live-updating app state leans Convex.

faqs.q: Which has the best free tier?
faqs.a: They limit different things. As of Nov 2026, Supabase Free includes a 500 MB database and 50,000 monthly active users but pauses inactive projects after a week; Firebase Spark has daily quotas such as 50K Firestore reads; Convex Free includes 1M function calls and 0.5 GB of database storage a month. Check each vendor's site for current pricing.

faqs.q: Which uses SQL?
faqs.a: Supabase, because each project is a Postgres database. Firebase's Firestore and Realtime Database are NoSQL, though Firebase also offers SQL Connect backed by Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL. Convex uses its own document database queried from TypeScript functions.

faqs.q: Do they include authentication?
faqs.a: Yes, all three list auth. Supabase Free includes 50,000 MAUs, Firebase Authentication is available on both plans with phone auth billed per SMS on Blaze, and Convex lists Auth on every plan.

faqs.q: Can I self-host any of them?
faqs.a: Supabase's pricing FAQ says you can self-host it for free with Docker or the Supabase CLI. Firebase is a Google-hosted service. Convex's pricing page doesn't cover self-hosting, so check its docs.
